# Release automation

Releases are published by the [Update Swift Package Version](release.yml) workflow, which runs daily and can also be triggered manually from the Actions tab.

Unlike the FullStory SDK, the SwiftUI selectors xcframework does not ship a `Package.swift` alongside it, so the manifest is generated by [`scripts/generate-package-swift.sh`](../../scripts/generate-package-swift.sh) rather than downloaded from the release server.

## What gates a release

The release server has no `VERSION` file specific to the selectors build, so the workflow reads the shared `VERSION` and only creates a release commit and tag once all of the following exist at that version:

- `fullstory-swiftui-selectors-<version>-xcframework.zip`
- `fullstory-<version>-xcframework.zip`
- the matching tag in `fullstory-swift-package-ios`

That last check matters because the generated manifest pins `fullstory-swift-package-ios` at exactly this version. That repo is updated by its own scheduled job, so a release server that is a few hours ahead of it would otherwise produce a package that cannot resolve.

If anything is missing the run exits successfully without changing the repo, so it is safe for the daily schedule to run while a release is still in progress. If a selectors release is ever skipped because the release server has already moved on to a newer `VERSION`, trigger the workflow manually and pass the version you want to publish.

## Keeping the tag and the branch together

A release is only complete when the tag and the default branch both point at the new manifest, so the two refs are pushed with `git push --atomic`: if either is rejected, neither lands, and there is no half-published release to clean up.

Each run also checks up front that the default branch contains the newest release tag and fails if it does not. Without that check a half-finished release would look done forever, because the duplicate-release check keys on the tag alone and would keep reporting success while the branch advertised a stale version. The comparison is by ancestry rather than equality, since the branch legitimately carries later commits such as workflow and README changes.

## Why the generated manifest looks the way it does

Two things about the manifest are deliberate and are worth knowing before changing the generator.

**No `platforms:` declaration.** Declaring one becomes a floor that every consuming package must also declare. Real apps keep SwiftUI code in packages that declare a lower deployment target or none at all, and SwiftPM would refuse to resolve those. The framework is currently built for iOS 13 and everything it exposes is guarded by `@available`, so it links at any deployment target.

**The `FSSwiftUISelectorsDependencies` target.** It contains no code. SwiftPM does not allow a binary target to declare dependencies, but the framework's `.swiftinterface` contains `import FullStory`, so consumers need the FullStory module on their search path and linked into their build. That empty target carries the FullStory dependency and ships as part of the `FSSwiftUISelectors` library product. Without it, a project that depends on this package alone fails to compile with `Unable to find module dependency: 'FullStory'`.
